overview: Emirate of Bin Shal'an is an imported atlas label, not a securely identified historical state. Its spelling resembles Ibn Sha'lan, the ruling house of the Ruwala confederation, and contemporary British records call Nuri al-Sha'lan the paramount Ruwala chief. Yet those same records place Ruwala movement from Hama and Homs through Azraq and Wadi Sirhan to al-Jawf. The atlas polygon excludes all those places. Instead it covers Riyadh, al-Hofuf, central Najd, and part of the Empty Quarter, remaining unchanged from 1920 through 1938. In 1938 it overlaps a Saudi Arabia feature, even though Saudi Arabia had been proclaimed in 1932. No reviewed source documents a central Arabian state called this name from 1920 to 1945. This card therefore preserves the imported alias while treating identification as disputed. It uses bounded evidence about Ruwala leadership and life, much of it from Alois Musil's outsider ethnography published in 1928 after earlier fieldwork. It does not assign those details to everyone inside the polygon. The 1945 disappearance is an editorial seam: Nuri died in 1942, the Ruwala and al-Sha'lan family continued, and Saudi Arabia did too.

periods.title: 1920 to 1923: al-Jawf is contested, not founded
periods.summary: A November 1920 report says Ibn Sha'lan tried and failed to capture al-Jawf. Later correspondence records rival sovereignty claims and negotiations involving Ibn Saud. These events concern a northern oasis and mobile confederation, while the atlas polygon begins far to the south around Riyadh and al-Hofuf.

periods.title: 1923 to 1926: borders harden around mobile lives
periods.summary: At the Kuwait Conference, an independent state under Ibn Sha'lan was proposed and rejected. The 1925 Hadda Agreement instead regulated a state boundary while protecting established grazing, residence, property, and movement. A debated diplomatic option should not be mistaken for a polity that actually occupied the atlas shape.

periods.title: 1926 to 1929: a book records mobile life imperfectly
periods.summary: Alois Musil published his large Rwala ethnography in 1928 from earlier fieldwork and oral evidence. It documents tents, food, kinship, children, water, and healing, but through an outsider's judgments and broad generalizations. Its details are bounded clues, not a census of 1928 or the atlas polygon.

periods.title: 1929 to 1932: dispute and accommodation cross borders
periods.summary: The Ruwala-Amarat camel dispute drew British and Saudi officials into negotiations while Fawwaz al-Sha'lan accompanied seasonal movement. Ruwala leaders also repaired relations with Ibn Saud. In 1931 the United States recognized Ibn Saud's Hejaz and Nejd government, which became Saudi Arabia in 1932.

periods.title: 1932 to 1935: alliance grows without territorial merger
periods.summary: Saudi Arabia now existed under that name, yet the atlas still displays the disputed Bin Shal'an feature alone. Scholarship traces continuing Ruwala autonomy and negotiation, followed by the 1935 marriage of Nuf bint Nawwaf al-Sha'lan to Ibn Saud. Kinship alliance did not turn one society into the other.

periods.title: 1935 to 1938: leadership links desert and cities
periods.summary: Nuri and Fawwaz worked through tribal relationships, Syrian politics, Saudi ties, and urban connections. A 1938 Kuwait list calls Fawwaz emir of the Ruwala, a title tied to people rather than this southern polygon. The year's atlas file introduces a separate Saudi Arabia shape over the same ground.

periods.title: 1938 to 1942: two atlas layers occupy one space
periods.summary: The unchanged Bin Shal'an polygon and Saudi Arabia overlap at Riyadh, al-Hofuf, central Najd, and the Empty Quarter. That cartographic contradiction prevents either feature from proving exclusive control. Nuri remained known as emir of the Ruwala until his death in 1942, far from a tidy map handover.

periods.title: 1942 to 1945: succession continues, then the label vanishes
periods.summary: After Nuri died, Fawwaz led the al-Sha'lan house and Ruwala relationships continued across state frontiers. The exact atlas id disappears in 1945 while Saudi Arabia remains. No reviewed evidence identifies a 1945 conquest or collapse matching that seam, so the ending belongs to the database.

items.text: The index imports the exact spelling Emirate of Bin Shal'an for approximately 1920 to 1945. Coverage finds three files and no existing card or reviewed summary. That establishes a database record, not the historical existence of a state, dynasty, capital, bureaucracy, or accepted border.

The target appears once in each of the 1920, 1930, and 1938 files. All three decode to the same 67-position Polygon, with the same bounds and coordinate hash. Unchanged geometry across changing politics is evidence of atlas reuse, not proof that one government held every point.

Riyadh, al-Hofuf, central Najd, and one Empty Quarter probe lie inside. Damascus, Homs, Azraq, northern Wadi Sirhan, Sakaka, al-Jawf, Hail, Mecca, Medina, Qatar, and Oman lie outside. The polygon therefore fails entirely to match documented Ruwala geography in the north.

In 1938 the target overlaps the separate Saudi Arabia feature at every tested interior point. Saudi Arabia had taken its name in 1932 and maintained international relations thereafter. The overlap is a neighboring-summary hazard: neither label may borrow the other card's government, people, or chronology.

Contemporary and institutional sources call Nuri bin Haza al-Sha'lan emir or paramount chief of the Ruwala. They do not securely identify a central Arabian polity named Emirate of Bin Shal'an. This card keeps the imported alias visible while declining to manufacture the missing state.

sections.title: Understand leadership without inventing a state

items.text: Musil describes chiefly standing as associated with prominent families, but leadership still depended on ability, support, consultation, and circumstances. A leader could not simply command a mobile confederation like a modern ministry. The account is an outsider's model, useful when kept beside diplomatic evidence and its limits.

The failed 1920 attempt on al-Jawf matters because it shows aspiration without possession. A report that Ibn Sha'lan attacked, lost, or negotiated over an oasis cannot establish a state stretching south through Riyadh. Military action is evidence of contest, not a deed to the atlas polygon.

At Kuwait, delegates discussed making an independent state under Ibn Sha'lan, but the proposal was rejected. Its appearance in conference minutes proves that officials imagined an option. It does not prove the option existed before the meeting, survived afterward, or had the polygon and dates imported here.

Ibn Saud's correspondence claimed Ruwala acknowledgment of his sovereignty while also revealing bargaining, personal contacts, and contested appointments. Because this is a ruler's diplomatic argument, it must be read as a claim made for a purpose. It neither erases Ruwala agency nor creates an al-Sha'lan state.

Contemporary biography describes Nuri working through Ruwala leadership and relationships with neighboring rulers and governments. His influence could be substantial without resembling exclusive territorial sovereignty. Power traveled through people, herds, kin, reputation, agreements, subsidies, and access rather than one solid color on a map.

sections.title: Move through pasture, water, and new borders

items.text: Musil distinguishes mobile herding from more settled livelihoods and ties movement to camels, pasture, water, and provisions. Those observations come from earlier fieldwork published in 1928. They illuminate Ruwala practice but cannot be assigned automatically to every family, every season, or anyone living inside the atlas polygon.

Camp sites were chosen with water, pasture, safety, and social grouping in view, according to Musil. Scouts could assess conditions before families moved. A campsite was therefore planned, not random wandering. Its temporary traces also make mobile competence less visible than stone walls in many historical records.

Taking down, loading, transporting, and rebuilding a tent coordinated people, camels, ropes, poles, fabric, and household equipment. Musil's detailed description shows practiced logistics. Mobility was work and knowledge, not simply absence from a town, and it required decisions that maps of fixed borders tend to hide.

The Hadda Agreement recognized established grazing, residence, and property interests across the new boundary while regulating movement and raiding. Its provisions show that officials could draw a line only by addressing lives already crossing it. Legal border making did not make seasonal geography vanish overnight.

British planners valued Wadi Sirhan for routes and believed influence there could affect Ruwala allegiance. That strategic argument belongs north of the imported polygon. It also warns against translating an archive's language of loyalty into permanent obedience by every camp, lineage, or traveler.

sections.title: Build tents, prepare food, and share work

items.text: Women produced and repaired black tent cloth from animal fiber, while poles, ropes, pegs, and repeated maintenance kept the structure useful. Musil records skilled labor rather than a disposable shelter. A tent could travel because considerable work had already been woven into every square of it.

Movable partitions divided guest and household spaces, and their arrangement could change with need. The source gives separate social zones without presenting a modern floor plan. Privacy, hospitality, gender, work, and sleep shared one adaptable structure whose walls could literally move when family life required it.

Wind direction and heat shaped where a tent opened and how its side cloths were placed. Families adjusted the structure rather than accepting whatever weather arrived. This was climate-responsive architecture with very fast renovation: no permit office, although camels and relatives could still complicate moving day.

Milk and grain anchored many meals in Musil's account, while availability changed with herds, trade, and season. Food shortage was a real risk. The evidence supports flexible preparation and careful use, not a single daily menu or the claim that all Ruwala families ate alike.

Edible plants and locusts widened the food supply when available. Musil's list is descriptive, sometimes judgmental, and not a nutrition survey. It nevertheless records alert use of changing environments, where knowing what could be gathered, prepared, traded, or saved mattered as much as owning livestock.

sections.title: Keep family and social life evidence-sized

items.text: Musil describes patrilineal kin groups while also calling a woman the mistress of her tent, responsible for substantial household property and work. His categories simplify lived relationships. The useful point is shared but unequal authority inside families, not a universal script for every marriage or household.

Birth narratives collected by Musil describe women relatives assisting and mothers naming newborns. They are intimate stories filtered through a male outsider and should not become a rule that no specialist helper ever attended. They show women's knowledge and support while leaving many experiences undocumented.

Inheritance rules in Musil's account connected property, descendants, and wider kin obligations. Written rules were not the only social force: negotiation, need, reputation, and relationships also mattered, though the page cannot recover every dispute. A summary of inheritance must remain narrower than a biography of family life.

Hospitality involved coffee, food, protection, and careful attention to a guest's standing and needs. These practices helped make social and political relationships. Coffee was not just a beverage break; it could announce welcome, obligation, conversation, and reputation, all inside a household whose resources were never unlimited.

Nuri acquired a Damascus residence around 1919 or 1920, and the Sha'lan name became attached to an urban district. That connection shows leading households moving between city and steppe. It should not turn all Ruwala into city residents or reduce mobile relatives to picturesque visitors.

sections.title: Let children learn without inventing schools

items.text: Musil says young children stayed close to mothers and gradually took on tasks involving animals, water, fire, and guests. Older boys also listened to adult discussion and learned poetry and public affairs. This is informal education through participation, not evidence for one fixed curriculum or age schedule.

Children ran, played group games, and joined sung gatherings. Musil records different activities for boys and girls but writes through his own social assumptions. Games offered exercise, practice, rhythm, cooperation, teasing, and fun, even though the source cannot tell us what every child preferred.

Researchers in 1934 and 1935 thanked Emir Fawwaz for hospitality while studying among the Ruwala and also acknowledged two doctors. The publication documents cooperation around research, not a tribal school system. It reminds us that named hosts and local participants shaped knowledge later printed under academic institutions.

Musil describes clerks using paper obtained from Damascus, reed pens, and ink for correspondence. Literacy was specialized and connected camps to cities. The presence of a clerk does not prove that children attended formal school, that everyone read Arabic, or that writing replaced oral teaching.

No secure exact-period written-language sample attributable to a Ruwala or al-Sha'lan author has been verified for this card. Musil's Latin-letter transcriptions preserve oral material through his scholarly system, not community-authored spelling. Printing generic Arabic here would substitute a language for a documented speaker, place, and text.

sections.title: Treat medicine, illness, and care cautiously

items.text: Musil records fevers, digestive illness, injuries, plant drinks, poultices, and splinting. Some actions were practical, others ritual, and the author judged them through early twentieth-century medicine. The list reveals attempts to relieve suffering, not modern proof that a remedy was safe, effective, or universally used.

For wounds, the source describes cleaning, dressings, and care by close relatives. A seriously ill person might rest in a separate tent, which could reduce disturbance or contact. The record supports nursing and isolation practices without proving a germ theory, standardized clinic, or consistent outcome.

Accounts of childbirth center women relatives and practical assistance, but Musil's access to women's experience was limited. A respectful history can recognize reproductive knowledge without claiming childbirth was easy, unattended, or identical. Maternal pain, loss, recovery, and individual choice are mostly silent in this source.

Water scarcity shaped washing, while sand, plant material, and soap could serve different cleaning tasks. Musil's language contains cultural prejudice, so concrete observations must be separated from his rankings. Scarcity required priorities; it does not justify treating a community as careless about bodies, clothes, or hospitality.

The university researchers who visited in the mid-1930s thanked physicians for medical assistance. That is evidence of some access around a particular field project, not a census of community health care. Family nursing, local remedies, urban doctors, and state services could overlap without forming one uniform system.

sections.title: Follow water, washing, waste, and absent toilets

items.text: Women could fetch nearby household water while herders managed supplies farther away, according to Musil. Distance, herd needs, weather, and the source shaped that division. Carrying water was daily infrastructure performed by people and animals, even when it left no pipe, pump house, or municipal record.

Hide bags, buckets, and troughs stored or moved water, and one large bag could hold a remarkable volume. Making, mending, filling, lifting, and guarding such equipment took skill. A waterskin had too important a job to spend its day pretending to be a shower.

Wells required drawing gear and coordinated camel watering. Order mattered when many animals arrived thirsty, because a damaged well or rushed herd could endanger everyone. Musil's description shows water management as social organization and animal handling, not merely the location of a blue dot on a map.

Large pools could serve people and animals while also collecting contamination. The source recognizes practical risk but does not document filtration or laboratory testing. Water quality depended on source, recent rain, crowding, and use. One pool cannot stand for every well, cistern, spring, or household container.

No reviewed source securely identifies a standard Ruwala latrine or toilet for 1920 to 1945. Mobile camps still required privacy and waste decisions, but inventing a structure would be false precision. Detailed tent inventories omit one, so the honest answer is an evidence gap rather than a joke about cleanliness.

sections.title: Notice skills, exchange, and small surprises

items.text: A tent's walls could be shifted as wind and sun changed, making the household architecture adjustable during the day. That flexibility was an achievement of material knowledge, weaving, and attention to weather. It also meant home improvement could happen with rope and cloth rather than a month of hammering.

Camps grouped related tents while balancing pasture, water, safety, and travel. After departure, ash, dung, and altered vegetation could mark occupation, but lightly built homes were easy for outsiders to underestimate. Archaeological visibility and social importance are different measures, especially in a mobile landscape.

Small amounts of water could rinse hands before a shared meal. The practice shows etiquette and cleaning adjusted to scarcity. It should not be expanded into a universal hygiene code, but it is a useful correction to stories that imagine desert hospitality without the ordinary details of preparing to eat.

Fawwaz accompanied seasonal migrations while also representing Ruwala interests in talks with officials. Moving with camps and negotiating in offices were not opposite careers. Leadership could require fluency in pasture conditions, kin relationships, diplomatic language, and the practical consequences of a line drawn across a migration route.

In 1935, Nuf bint Nawwaf al-Sha'lan married Ibn Saud, creating a significant kinship alliance. The marriage connected political houses but did not merge every Ruwala household into the Saudi state or validate the atlas polygon. Family ties could bridge power centers while preserving distinct identities and interests.

sections.title: End the card without ending the people

items.text: The 1938 Kuwait list identifies Fawwaz as emir of the Ruwala, not sovereign of a central Arabian polygon. Titles such as emir can describe leadership without proving modern territorial statehood. Translation, audience, and context matter before a title becomes a border, dynasty, or constitutional office.

Nuri died in 1942, three years before the atlas removes the feature. Fawwaz and the al-Sha'lan family continued public roles, and Ruwala networks persisted across Syria, Jordan, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia. A leader's death changed relationships, but it did not erase a people or explain the 1945 seam.

The exact id is absent in 1945 while Saudi Arabia remains. No geometry morphs, no successor link is encoded, and no reviewed source records a matching 1945 annexation. The safest ending is continuity: the database stopped drawing one disputed label while documented communities and states continued.

Achievement here lies in sustaining mobile households, water logistics, herds, hospitality, kin obligations, negotiation, and exchange across newly enforced borders. These accomplishments belong to Ruwala people where the evidence supports them. They should not be awarded to everyone inside a mismatched polygon or converted into imperial nostalgia.

The card leaves predecessors and successors empty because neither neighboring atlas labels nor family succession establishes political identity. Arabia (Nejd), Saudi Arabia, Hail, and Hejaz have their own histories. Linking them automatically would hide the very contradiction this research uncovered and could spread borrowed summaries into future cards.

ending.text: The 1945 endpoint is an editorial atlas seam, not a securely documented political fall. The disputed feature disappears while Saudi Arabia remains, three years after Nuri al-Sha'lan's death. Ruwala families, the al-Sha'lan house, cross-border relationships, mobile knowledge, and urban ties continued. No reviewed evidence supports a 1945 conquest, dissolution, or population ending that matches this polygon.
